clue.text: More than one House of Lords soliloquy's beginning: "Let Tom Hayes go free"

definitions.text: More than one House of Lords

indicators.note: the beginning of the word soliloquy's gives its opening letter only
letters set free from their order can be rearranged, so the name Let Tom Hayes is reshuffled

explanation.surface: A peer's dramatic speech in the Lords pleads for the release of a prisoner called Tom Hayes.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads 'House' as a lord's home rather than the chamber. The S from 'soliloquy's beginning' comes first, then 'go free' rearranges LETTOMHAYES.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand country mansions are the ancestral houses of aristocratic families, so several of them are houses belonging to lords.

clue.text: Acrobat ends with somersault into wagon

indicators.note: the end of the word turns head over heels, so only its last letters are read backwards

parts.note: a tumbler is an acrobat who performs flips and rolls

explanation.surface: A circus acrobat finishes the act by flipping into a cart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ends with somersault' turns round only the last three letters of TUMBLER, so LER becomes REL.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbrel is a two-wheeled cart, famous for carrying condemned prisoners to the guillotine, so it is a kind of wagon.

clue.text: Huge number working to support Turkey, Italy turn up sick

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath the rest, so it comes last

parts.note: TR is the international vehicle code for Turkey
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word sick's synonym is read from bottom to top

parts.note: sick means ill
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: Something about an enormous sum being needed to prop up ailing economies in Turkey and Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn up' reverses ILL to LLI; 'to support' puts ON at the bottom of this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A trillion is a million million, so it is a vast figure.

clue.text: Admire Liberal 50s President

parts.note: Ike was the nickname of Dwight Eisenhower, US President through the 1950s

explanation.surface: A liberal voter expresses admiration for Eisenhower.
explanation.definitionFit: To like someone is to be fond of them, a milder form of admiring.

clue.text: From a noble family — a Chinese dynasty — superior to Scotsman

parts.note: the Han dynasty ruled China for four centuries
superior to means over, in the sense of higher in rank or position
Ian is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: A genealogy claims descent from both Chinese emperors and Scottish lairds.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hanoverians were the royal house that gave Britain its Georges and Victoria, so the adjective describes that dynasty.

clue.text: Whoa … strangely into Mark's ridiculous hairstyle

indicators.note: into means the shuffled letters go inside the abbreviation

parts.note: MK is a standard abbreviation for mark, as in the German currency

indicators.note: strangely means the word Whoa is set out in an odd new order

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in shock at Mark's absurd new haircut.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation in the surface is really anagram fodder: 'strangely' makes OHAW from it, which 'into' sets inside Mark's abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mohawk (Mohican in Britain) is a shaved head with a central strip of upright hair, often thought outlandish.

clue.text: Sun copy editor put pen to paper

parts.note: to crib is to copy someone else's work

explanation.surface: An editor at The Sun newspaper finally writes something down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun' looks like the tabloid paper, which makes 'copy editor' read as a newspaper job.
explanation.definitionFit: Scribed is the past tense of scribe, to write, which is what putting pen to paper does.

clue.text: "Don is masterly when aroused" — actress

indicators.note: arousing stirs things up, so the words Don is masterly are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A quote boasting of a man named Don's prowess in bed, attributed to a performer.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Don' is Donald Trump, whose alleged affair with this adult-film actress became a court case.
explanation.definitionFit: Stormy Daniels is the stage name of an American adult-film performer, so she is an actress.

clue.text: Crystal Maze screening live piece, illegally transmitting online

indicators.note: screening means hiding something behind or within, so one piece holds another
a maze twists paths about, so the word Crystal is twisted into a new order

parts.note: to live is to be, to exist
the king is a chess piece

explanation.surface: The TV game show The Crystal Maze is broadcast, with a segment on online offences.
explanation.walkthrough: The Crystal Maze was a British TV game show, but here 'Maze' is the anagram signal, giving CYRSTAL, which 'screening' splits to hold the verb for live.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyberstalking is the criminal harassment of someone through the internet, typically by sending threatening messages.

clue.text: Whittington, chasing cat, ran hard all over the place with unknown, random blokes

indicators.note: chasing means following, so this name comes after the cat

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
Dick Whittington, Lord Mayor of London in folklore, famously had a cat

indicators.note: letters all over the place are in disorder, so ran hard is rearranged

parts.note: Y is one of the letters used for an unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.surface: Dick Whittington runs frantically after his cat, joined by a crowd of nobodies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all over the place' rearranges RANHARD to ANDHARR.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom, Dick and Harry is an idiom for any ordinary people at all, chosen without distinction.

clue.text: Bloody lavatory emptied once in a blue moon

parts.note: meat cooked bloody is rare

indicators.note: a word emptied loses its contents, keeping only the outside letters

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a horrible toilet is only cleared out very occasionally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' is a British intensifier in the surface, but here describes a steak.
explanation.definitionFit: Once in a blue moon is an idiom for something that happens very seldom.

clue.text: I could swear it's a Volkswagen, empty, going round Elba

indicators.note: going round suggests letters circling and landing in a new order

parts.note: VW is the badge and abbreviation of Volkswagen
empty means nothing, which is the letter O

explanation.surface: A tourist drives an empty Beetle around the island of Elba.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' looks like a drive round the island, but it signals a rearrangement of every piece before it, the car badge and the nothing included.
explanation.definitionFit: Something avowable can be openly declared or sworn to, so a speaker could vouch for it.

clue.text: Two Frenchmen in disgrace, sent off having participated in brawl

indicators.note: in means the pair of Frenchmen are placed within the rearranged letters
sent off suggests letters dispatched and scattered, so disgrace is rearranged

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for monsieur, so two of them make MM

explanation.surface: Two French footballers are sent off in disgrace after joining a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent off' reads as a red card, but it rearranges the word before it into SCRIAGED, and 'in' sets the two monsieurs inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrimmage is a confused scuffle, so to have scrimmaged is to have taken part in a scrappy fight.

clue.text: New York taxi driver's first caution

parts.note: New York cabs are famously painted yellow, so one is a yellow car

indicators.note: the first of the word driver's is just its opening letter

explanation.surface: A New York cabbie gets a warning, maybe from police.
explanation.walkthrough: A yellow card is shown by a football referee to warn a player.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a referee shows a yellow card as a formal warning to a player, which is called a caution.

clue.text: 13th or 15th? That is before time

indicators.note: before means only the letters coming ahead of the time abbreviation are kept

parts.note: id est is the Latin for that is, abbreviated i.e.

explanation.surface: A question about dates, answered with a clarification about timing.
explanation.walkthrough: Spell out 'That is' in full Latin, ID EST, and keep what comes before its final T.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the Ides fell on the 15th of March, May, July and October, and the 13th of other months.

clue.text: Where cider is drunk, luring in Liverpool banker endlessly

indicators.note: luring in means drawing something inside, so the drunk surrounds the river

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunk

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter of the river's name is dropped

parts.note: a river has banks, so the Mersey, Liverpool's river, is a banker

explanation.surface: A cider-drinker tempts a Liverpool bank employee into joining the session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where cider is drunk' looks like the whole definition, but 'drunk' is the SOT. 'banker' is crossword slang for a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset is an English county in the West Country famous for its orchards and cider making.

clue.text: Being mischievous, skipping first half of study

indicators.note: skipping the first half means the opening four of eight letters are left out

parts.note: research is careful study

explanation.surface: A pupil playing up by skipping half the homework.
explanation.definitionFit: Arch as an adjective means playfully knowing or roguish, as in an arch smile.

clue.text: Film actors entertaining fashionable eastern movie buff

indicators.note: entertaining means hosting, so the cast holds the other letters inside

parts.note: the actors in a film are its cast
in means fashionable

explanation.surface: Film stars host a stylish fan from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: A cineast (or cineaste) is an enthusiast of the cinema, a film devotee.

clue.text: A bit of syrup in a cola daiquiri (a rum cocktail)

indicators.note: a bit of means only a part of the following run of words is taken

explanation.surface: A recipe note about adding syrup to a cola and daiquiri mix.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed words, read as an aside, are the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A piña colada is a rum drink blended with pineapple juice and coconut cream.

clue.text: Jane, Molly, Ida, Ena regularly getting out of the wind

indicators.note: letters getting out at regular intervals means every second letter is taken from the names

explanation.surface: Four women escape a gale together.
explanation.definitionFit: Aeolian means relating to or carried by the wind, after Aeolus, the Greek god of winds.

clue.text: Hit Sierra, then three-wheeler

parts.note: Sierra is S in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a trike is a tricycle, with three wheels

explanation.surface: A car collision: first a Ford Sierra, then a tricycle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sierra was a popular Ford family car in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike someone is to hit them.

clue.text: It's pub-o'clock; get a round in, sharpish!

indicators.note: in means the round goes inside the other letters

parts.note: when the drinking hour comes, it is time at the inn
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: A drinker announces it is time for the pub and urges someone to buy drinks quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' looks like a round of drinks but is the shape O.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharpish is British informal for quickly, and doing something immediately is the same idea.

clue.text: Take the Mickey out of British comeback kid at first

parts.note: read as come back, the word come is written backwards

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letter of kid is used

explanation.surface: A British sportsman returning to the game is mocked from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comeback' splits as 'come back': COME written backwards. Taking the Mickey is British slang for teasing.
explanation.definitionFit: To bemock is an old word for to ridicule, which is what taking the Mickey means.

clue.text: Nobleman expected to receive his king

indicators.note: to receive means the word for expected takes the king inside it

parts.note: something due is expected
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: An aristocrat awaits a visit from his monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A duke is the highest rank of the British peerage below royalty.

clue.text: A starter for 10 likely to be ruled out of court?

definitions.meaning: on the British quiz show University Challenge, the opening question is announced as a starter for ten, so it is the question that leads

definitions.text: likely to be ruled out of court?
definitions.meaning: in court a question that steers a witness to an answer is objected to and disallowed

explanation.surface: A quiz question about whether an argument would be thrown out by a judge.
explanation.definitionFit: A question prompting the desired reply is inadmissible in examination, and a quiz's first question opens the round.

clue.text: Retirement finally, Roger, stop compiling crosswords, giving others inspiration!

indicators.note: finally means just the last letter of the word Retirement

parts.note: in radio talk Roger means received, abbreviated R
to end something is to stop it
a crossword compiler is called a setter, so compiling is setting

explanation.surface: A crossword setter announces retirement and urges others to take up the craft.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a farewell note from the setter himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Trendsetting describes leading the way so that others follow and copy, which is inspiring them.
